title: High-risk drinking falls among Korean men, but climbs for women
summary:
The past decade has seen high-risk drinking rates fall among Korean men of all age groups, while women over the age of 30 are actually drinking more, according to new data released by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA).

The post High-risk drinking falls among Korean men, but climbs for women appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
The past decade has seen high-risk drinking rates fall among Korean men of all age groups, while women over the age of 30 are actually drinking more, according to new data released by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA). For men, the findings define high-risk drinking as seven or more shots of soju or five or more cans of beer in a single sitting, whereas for women, the threshold is five or more shots of soju or three or more cans of beer. The research is based on the 2025 Community Health Survey, an annual poll which queries around 230,000 adults aged 13 and older to gauge information about health and chronic disease. The data showed that more than half (57.1%) of Korean adults drank at least once a month, while 33.7% binge drank and 12% engaged in high-risk drinking. However, drinking habits sharply differed by age and gender.

Half of Korean men binge drink, says study

Between 2016 and 2025, the high-risk drinking rate dropped across all age groups for men, from those in their 20s to those 70 and older. In the same time period, the high-risk drinking rate shot up in every age group for women, with the exception of those in their 20s. Despite this, men still outpaced women on every indicator, with middle-aged men in particular prone to problematic drinking. Half of men in their 30s, 40s and 50s binge drank and more than one in five in their 40s and 50s engaged in high-risk drinking. Among women, binge drinking peaked among those in their 20s at 34.2%, followed by those in their 30s at 26.6%. As judged by SBS News, the rise in older women’s drinking rates may have been driven by the expansion of social activities for women including dining out and gatherings, the diversification of drinking methods, with drinking alone and at home now more common, as well as changes in the  social perception of women’s drinking.

What about people drinking less?

And while these statistics point to a prevalence in harmful drinking behaviours, an alternative movement is seeing young Koreans get curious about sobriety, with non-alcoholic beer spending rising by almost a third over the past three years, the drinks business previously reported. This might explain why it's only among women aged 30+ that drinking rates have climbed up. South Korea’s household alcohol spend saw its sharpest sharpest drop in seven years in the first quarter of this year, with more than half of Korea’s pubs vanishing over the past eight years, thanks to elevated operating costs, and the fall of after-work drinks gatherings – no longer the corporate tradition they once were. Shipments of diluted soju, South Korea’s best-known spirit, also fell by 13.4% between 2019 and 2025, according to the National Tax Service. Volumes declined from 916,000 kilolitres to 793,000 kilolitres over the six-year period. Although shipments briefly recovered in 2022 as Covid restrictions eased, rising 4.3% year-on-year to 862,000 kilolitres, the broader downward trend has continued, pointing to a broader national shift in drinking habits.

title: Champagne and Cognac lift Moët Hennessy as LVMH returns to growth
summary:
LVMH's wines and spirits division returned to growth in the first half of 2026, with Champagne and Cognac showing signs of recovery after two difficult years and helping to drive an improved performance across the luxury group.

The post Champagne and Cognac lift Moët Hennessy as LVMH returns to growth appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
LVMH's wines and spirits division returned to growth in the first half of 2026, with Champagne and Cognac showing signs of recovery after two difficult years and helping to drive an improved performance across the luxury group. LVMH's Wines & Spirits division delivered one of the strongest performances across the luxury conglomerate during the first half of 2026, as Champagne and Cognac rebounded despite continued geopolitical and economic uncertainty. Organic revenue in the division rose 5% during the first six months of the year, with profit from recurring operations climbing 11% to €582 million. The improvement came as the wider LVMH group reported revenue of €38.6 billion, down 3% on a reported basis but up 2% organically, with second-quarter growth accelerating to 3%. Group operating profit slipped 4% to €8.7 billion, although net profit remained broadly unchanged at €5.7 billion.

Recovery for Champagne and Cognac

LVMH said its Champagne business showed "encouraging signs", particularly for prestige cuvées, after two years in which the category has faced softer global demand. Moët & Chandon also completed its second season as the Official Champagne of Formula 1, continuing the brand's renewed marketing push. Cognac also showed signs of improvement. The group said Hennessy maintained the positive momentum seen during Chinese New Year, helping offset continued uncertainty in other markets. LVMH also expanded the Hennessy brand in the United States with the launch of its V.S. ready-to-serve cocktail range. Elsewhere within the portfolio, Provence rosé wines continued to post growth, with LVMH saying brand desirability, innovation and disciplined cost control remained priorities for the division.

Confidence returns

Commenting on the results, chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault said: "LVMH demonstrated its solidity and effective strategy. Our Maisons, which remained focused on ensuring the utmost quality in our products, and several of which are pursuing their creative renewal, continued to inspire dreams and enhance their desirability." Arnault added that "the recovery in champagne and cognac" had contributed to stronger second-quarter momentum and said the group was entering the second half of the year with "renewed confidence".

Long-awaited turnaround

The improved performance marks a notable change for Moët Hennessy after a prolonged slowdown that has fuelled questions over the future of the division. As previously reported by the drinks business, speculation earlier this year suggested Diageo could sell its 34% stake in Moët Hennessy as part of a wider portfolio reshuffle. The FTSE 100 drinks group swiftly dismissed the reports, insisting it had "no intention" of selling either Guinness or its minority holding in the LVMH-owned wines and spirits business.

title: Wente Family Estates officially appoints new CEO
summary:
Following a "brief but productive" tenure as Wente's interim CEO since January, Peter Yeung will become the permanent chief exec of the Californian winery, thought to be the longest continuously family-run and operated producer in the US.

The post Wente Family Estates officially appoints new CEO appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Following a "brief but productive" tenure as Wente's interim CEO since January, Peter Yeung will become the permanent chief exec of the Californian winery, thought to be the longest continuously family-run and operated producer in the US.  

Peter Yeung will step up as Wente Family Estate's official new CEO with immediate effect after "successfully guiding the historic estate's strategic operations" since January 2026, the company said.

Yeung will oversee all aspects of the Californian wine producer based in Livermore Valley, including viticulture, winemaking, global sales, marketing, and hospitality for its portfolio of brands, which includes Wente Vineyards, Murrieta's Well, and the new Cresta Blanca, the launch of which Yeung oversaw in May. “It’s an honour to steward Wente Family Estates alongside the fourth and fifth generations of the Wente family, carrying on the values of quality, value, innovation, and stewardship of the land that have helped this winery span 143 years (and counting),” commented Yeung. “I look forward to continuing to work alongside current and future generations of the Wente family and our incredibly talented team to build on this winery’s rich heritage while driving innovation, deepening our commitment to sustainability, and expanding our global reach.”

Brief but productive

Prior to Yeung's "brief but productive tenure" as interim CEO, Yeung served on the winery’s advisory board, "providing valuable counsel" to the company’s senior leadership team, said Christine Wente, chairman of the board.

“Peter’s steady leadership, strategic mind, and boundless energy are tremendous assets for our winery,” she continued.

Before joining Wente Family Estates, Yeung co-author the book Luxury Wine Marketing, and co-hosted wine business podcast XChateau. He was also vice president of strategy and business development at prestigious Californian estates Realm Cellars in Napa Valley and Kosta Browne in Sonoma.

Shake-up

Yeung’s appointment comes amidst a raft of other changes to the senior leadership team, including Aly Wente’s appointment to the role of chief revenue officer and Karl Wente to the new role of chief operating officer. Niki Wente continues to serve as director of viticulture, while Jordan Wente works as senior brand ambassador.

"Our family and team provide a multi-generational perspective that enables our success for the decades ahead," said Christine Wente.

Founded in 1883, Wente Family Estates is thought to be the longest continuously family-owned and operated winery in the US. The winery owns certified sustainable vineyards in the Livermore Valley, San Francisco Bay, and Arroyo Seco, Monterey appellations. Wente Family Estates is also the US importer for Champagne Castelnau, Blanchard Perez, Blanchard & Lurton, and Bodega Cuarto Dominio.

title: Exceptionally rare 1811 Riesling comes up for auction
summary:
A bottle of 1811 Forster Ungeheuer Riesling, thought to be the oldest  bottle of German Riesling from a named single vineyard to ever be offered at a European auction, is being auctioned by Amsterdam-based online marketplace Catawiki - a wine made in the year that Sense & Sensibility was published.

The post Exceptionally rare 1811 Riesling comes up for auction appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: A bottle of 1811 Forster Ungeheuer Riesling, thought to be the oldest  bottle of German Riesling from a named single vineyard to ever be offered at a European auction, is being auctioned by Amsterdam-based online marketplace Catawiki - a wine made in the year that Sense & Sensibility was published. The exceptionally rare 1811 Forster Ungeheuer Riesling from renowned Pfalz winery Weingut Bassermann-Jordan, is the only one of eight remaining bottles to be auctioned in the sale that runs from 24 July to 3 August. It has a pre-sale estimate of €10,000–€13,000. The bottle come direct from the winery's historic cellar, where it has remained for more than 200 years. It has recently been recorked (April 2026), being preserved exclusively with wine from the same 1811 vintage, with no younger wine added. Although it is not the oldest Riesling to be sold at auction - a half-bottle of Rüdesheimer Riesling from the 1727 vintages was sold by Christie’s in May 2009 – it is thought to be the oldest full bottle that originates from a documented single vineyard, one that comes directly from the winery's historic cellar, and is preserved exclusively with wine from its original vintage. The winery is located in the village of Forst an der Weinstraße, part of the Mittelhaardt region of the Pfalz wine area, coming from the 38-hectare vineyard. The 1811 vintage was, according to Catawiki, one of Europe's most celebrated historic vintages - a famous 'comet vintage' which coincided with the appearance of the  Flaugergues comet, following a string of bad vintages at the start of the 19th century. A tasting organised to celebrate the winery's 300th anniversary in 2018 saw Anne Krebiehl MW describe it as "remarkably fresh and balanced", despite it being more than two centuries old. Catawiki specialises in art, design, jewellery, fashion, classic cars and collectables.

title: Discover a brand that is ‘a complete Spanish wine universe’
summary:
Pata Negra showcases the true diversity of Spain. With wines from many regions, it offers an opportunity for consumers to explore Spain through a single portfolio. db reports.

The post Discover a brand that is ‘a complete Spanish wine universe’ appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Pata Negra showcases the true diversity of Spain. With wines from many regions, it offers an opportunity for consumers to explore Spain through a single portfolio. db reports. Pata Negra is interesting because it brings together two qualities that are not always easy to combine: strong Spanish authenticity and broad international accessibility. It is a brand rooted in Spain’s wine culture, but it speaks in a clear, modern and approachable way to consumers around the world. J García Carrión's vice president Luciano García Carrión says: “What makes Pata Negra special is that it is not built around one single region, one single style or one single occasion. It is a complete Spanish wine universe. Through Pata Negra, consumers can discover the richness of Spain’s most important appellations, from the elegance of Rioja to the power of Toro, the freshness of Rueda, the generosity of La Mancha and the Mediterranean character of Cava.”

Diversity

Spain is one of the most diverse wine-producing countries in the world, but for many consumers that diversity can feel complex. Pata Negra helps to simplify that journey and in this sense is also a storytelling platform As García Carrión suggests: “Every appellation contributes something different: landscape, grape variety, climate, tradition and personality. The brand brings all of those elements together under one identity, making Spanish wine more understandable and more exciting for international consumers.” In Rioja, Pata Negra expresses the elegance and balance for which the region is famous. In Toro, the brand shows a completely different side of Spain. In Rueda, Pata Negra moves into freshness and aromatic expression. In La Mancha, Pata Negra demonstrates the scale, versatility and modern potential of Spain’s largest vineyard area.

Premium expressions

“The portfolio also extends into other styles, including sparkling wines from Cava, showing that Pata Negra is not only about red wine. It covers still and sparkling wines, whites, reds and rosés, young wines and aged wines, everyday wines and more premium expressions,” says García Carrión, before adding: “Pata Negra is not limited to one expression. It gives consumers a broad but coherent view of Spain.”

Pata Negra Toro

This wine “unleashes a resplendent bouquet of dark cherries, plums and wild flowers”, says Luciano García Carrión, noting that it offers up “black cherries, smoky oak and a hint of cigar”, which manage to “intertwine with earthy tea leaves and mineral depth”. Ultimately, it is a wine that is “powerful, yet refined, with firm tannins and a long, spicy finish. A bold, untamed expression of Toro,” he says.

title: Bondi Beach brew Fellr goes national
summary:
Popular RTD soda brand Fellr partners with Australian Vintage to distribute its youth-oriented drinks across the country. Rebecca Lo reports.

The post Bondi Beach brew Fellr goes national appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Popular RTD soda brand Fellr partners with Australian Vintage to distribute its youth-oriented drinks across the country. Rebecca Lo reports. Fellr is joining forces with Australian Vintage to expand its RTD alcoholic sodas nationally across Australia. Starting 1 August, Fellr will leverage the ASX-listed wine and drinks company’s extensive network to expand from its Sydney base, with Australian Vintage managing its national sales. Fellr was founded in a Bondi garage by Will Morgan and Andy Skora in 2020 and has quickly gained a following for its brewed alcoholic sodas. Canned for convenient pursuit of lifestyle pastimes, it has tapped into youth culture through its music, surf, fashion and art collaborations.

Expanded national footprint

Fellr’s range of beverages is made with natural fruit flavours and includes pink lemonade, ginger beer and watermelon vodka ranging from 4 to 6.5 ABV. Its Alfred’s Apartment Lemon Squash was recognised at The World Premix Awards 2025; more recently in June 2026, Fellr signed exclusive pours with Venues NSW in four iconic stadiums, adding to two others in New South Wales where it is already available.  Fellr’s partnership with Australian Vintage offers the independent brand the ability to scale up across the country and strengthen its retail presence including its ambition to expand its vodka-based RTDs and full bottled spirits. For Australian Vintage, Fellr supports its mandate to drive growth through innovation.  

Building momentum

“This partnership with Australian Vintage gives us the opportunity to build on the momentum we’ve created, strengthen our off-premise presence, support our retail partners, and make Fellr more accessible to consumers across Australia,” said Morgan.  “We’re hugely excited about what’s ahead and confident Australian Vintage is the right partner to help take the brand to the next level,” said Skora. “Partnering with Fellr was an easy decision,” said Tom Dusseldorp, CEO with Australian Vintage. “To build a brand from nothing and maintain consumer love over some of the toughest competitive times in RTD show that the guys have created something special. It is a privilege to drive the brand from here, and we look forward to expanding our portfolio in a very considered way to ensure we are providing retailers with curated and consumer backed brands.”

title: Damm takes stake in Dalston’s Soda
summary:
Damm UK has made its first soft drinks partner London-founded Dalston's Soda Co, marking another step in the company’s journey to diversify its drinks portfolio. Jessica Mason reports.

The post Damm takes stake in Dalston’s Soda appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Damm UK has made its first soft drinks partner London-founded Dalston's Soda Co, marking another step in the company’s journey to diversify its drinks portfolio. Jessica Mason reports. The deal, which Damm has confirmed to the drinks business is "a minority stake" without disclosing the investment figure, will see production move to Damm Eagle Brewery in Bedford and also coincides with a time Damm is "strategically expanding" after the business ended 2025 with revenue of €2.01 billion while also boosting capacity in the UK.

The opportunity

The partnership also follows Damm's acquisition of the Old Speckled Hen brands earlier this month and assists Damm on its path to becoming a "total beverage company" as well as offering Dalston’s Soda an avenue to accelerate its growth nationally. The terms of the new agreement will also see Damm support Dalston’s Soda Co across production, distribution and commercial infrastructure to further Dalston's growth across on-trade and off-trade channels.

Alignment

Dalston’s Soda, which is certified with B Corp status and makes its drinks with real fruit, no added sugar and without artificial sweeteners or flavourings, were all attributes that Damm has said resonate with its own values since they focus on quality, natural ingredients, craftsmanship and authenticity. Dalston’s B Corp status, according to the firm, also appeals since it complements Damm’s values rooted in sustainability. Other virtues of the partnership are that both businesses have established strong relationships with gastronomy and hospitality. Additionally, Damm also fosters ties with the fields of culture, sport and music, offering Dalston’s future avenues for connection.

'Like-minded'

Speaking to db, Damm UK managing director Luke White said: "Taking a stake in Dalston's broadens Damm's portfolio with a like-minded brand that shares our focus on quality, craftsmanship and authenticity. Alongside our recent acquisition of the Old Speckled Hen family of brands and our long-term distribution partnership with Northern Monk, we're building a stronger portfolio that speaks to the British consumer, with each bringing something different to our offering both in the UK and internationally. Together, these partnerships are helping put Damm UK on the path to becoming a total beverage company, mirroring the way Damm operates in Spain.” White also revealed to db that Damm has “seen a 20% year-on-year increase in branded volume within our UK portfolio – a clear signal that consumer preference is shifting towards more premium products” and admitted “we expect that trend to continue”.

'Respect for gastronomy, sustainability and the arts'

Commenting on the deal, Dalston’s Soda Co founder Duncan O’Brien said: “It’s a little mind-blowing to see Dalston’s make it from its bootstrapped origins to partnering with Damm. They’re a superb ally for Dalston’s - we share a focus on producing great-tasting drinks, and a real respect for gastronomy, sustainability and the arts. It’s a huge vote of confidence in what we’ve built, and we’re thrilled at the growth potential that working with the Damm team brings.”

'Strong strategic synergy'

White told db: “Dalston's, as a premium, founder-led brand with strong strategic synergy, represents an attractive investment opportunity with significant growth potential, particularly as consumers continue to moderate their alcohol intake and increasingly seek out natural, ingredient-led products." In a recent interview with db, White had hinted at the soft drinks category being one area Damm had seen promise and had highlighted that it was a "category that sits there and has been innovating for ages, but no one’s really taken any notice of soft drinks innovation".

Unlocking potential

Dalston’s Soda Co chairman Giles Brook added: “We are incredibly excited to be partnering with Damm. As they continue to broaden their total beverage offering, we believe Dalston’s can play a significant role as their core soft drinks proposition, providing trade customers with an exciting, natural, healthier alternative to traditional soft drinks while delivering the bold, exceptional fruit flavours that consumers increasingly seek. We believe this partnership represents a hugely exciting opportunity to accelerate Dalston’s growth and unlock the brand’s full potential. We look forward to building something truly special together.”

title: US expansion boosts Chapel Down sales
summary:
Chapel Down has reported a 19% rise in net sales revenue for the first half of 2026, with the English wine producer citing gains across every channel and accelerating momentum in the US market.

The post US expansion boosts Chapel Down sales appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Chapel Down has reported a 19% rise in net sales revenue for the first half of 2026, with the English wine producer citing gains across every channel and accelerating momentum in the US.

In a trading update released this morning, England's largest winemaker said Net sales revenue (NSR) reached £9.4 million for the six months to 30 June 2026, up from £7.9 million a year earlier, in line with management's expectations.

H1 2026 at a glance

Metric H1 2026 H1 2025 Change
Total NSR £9.4m £7.9m +19%
Off-trade NSR £4.4m £3.7m* +18%
On-trade NSR £1.5m £1.3m* +18%
On-trade outlets 2,750 2,597 +6%
International NSR £0.8m £0.5m* +66%
International markets 19 16 +3
Direct-to-consumer NSR £2.5m £2.4m* +4%
DTC returning customer rate 63% 62% +1pt
Net debt £14.0m £11.3m +£2.7m
Traditional Method share of wine NSR 74% 70% +4pts
Price index vs Champagne 92% 92% flat
Brand awareness 46% 46% flat

*Prior-year channel figures calculated from the reported percentage growth (original not disclosed in absolute terms).

Off-trade sales climbed 18% to £4.4 million, with the group saying it extended its lead in the English sparkling wine category, which itself grew at double-digit rates over the period. On-trade NSR also rose 18%, to £1.5 million, on the back of a 6% increase in unique outlets, to 2,750.

The standout was international, where NSR jumped 66% to £0.8 million. Chapel Down said its US partnership with Jackson Family Wines was gathering momentum, with the brand now stocked in 31 states and newly listed in 250 Whole Foods Market stores nationwide. The group ended the period trading in 19 international markets, up from 16 a year earlier.

Direct-to-consumer sales grew a more modest 4% to £2.5 million, with 3,838 new customers added to the group's own-brand website and the returning customer rate ticking up to 63%.

Net debt increased to £14.0 million (FY2025: £12.4 million), which the company attributed to its disciplined capital allocation policy. During H1, Chapel Down extended its Revolving Credit Facility from £20 million to £25 million, with a further £5 million accordion option available to take the facility to £30 million.

Premiumisation continues

The group said its premiumisation strategy continued to bear fruit, with traditional method sparkling now accounting for 74% of wine NSR, up from 70% a year earlier, while its price index against Champagne held steady at 92%.

Chapel Down also pointed to a string of new partnerships, including deals with The Jockey Club – covering Cheltenham, Epsom and Newmarket racecourses – and the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, alongside a three-year renewal of its Ascot partnership. The company said sales at Royal Ascot saw 45% value growth year-on-year, helped by the launch of a Rosé Magnum.

Brand awareness held at 46%, still the highest of any English Sparkling Wine brand, according to the group. Chapel Down also picked up nine Gold awards, while its Tenterden Brand Home — boosted by a new tasting room in Hythe — lifted its TripAdvisor rating to 4.8.

Outlook for 2026

Looking ahead, Chapel Down said growing conditions in Kent had been mixed, with a late May frost followed by warm, sunny weather. The board expects overall yield to be broadly in line with the five-year average, with a further update to follow closer to harvest.

The company said it remains confident of delivering full-year results in line with market expectations, which it disclosed as NSR of £22.1 million and Adjusted EBITDA (excluding the fair value adjustment on biological produce) of £3.7 million for FY2026.

James Pennefather, chief executive of Chapel Down, said: "Chapel Down's strong momentum in 2025 has continued into 2026 with +19% topline growth in H1, as we took market share in a growing category. We continue to be encouraged by the positive market dynamics we are seeing in the UK: increased adoption by Millennials and the continued expansion of high value sparkling occasions away from their historic heartland of formal celebration occasions."

Continuing he said, "Significant progress is being made in the US, where consumers are embracing the crisp, fresh style of sparkling wine that is our signature. With 1,000 acres of vineyards in Kent, Chapel Down has established itself as the leading brand in this exciting emerging category, and we remain confident that this provides a strong foundation for continued double digit growth."

title: Rémy Cointreau first quarter sales up as Cognac rebounds
summary:
Rémy Cointreau has posted first-quarter sales of €223.2 million, up 1.3% on an organic basis, with Cognac driving growth while its liqueurs and spirits division declined.

The post Rémy Cointreau first quarter sales up as Cognac rebounds appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Rémy Cointreau has confirmed its full-year objectives for 2026-27 after posting first-quarter sales of €223.2 million, up 1.3% on an organic basis, with Cognac driving growth while its liqueurs and spirits division declined.

The French drinks group reported sales growth of 1.1% for the April-June period, with a slight negative currency effect of -0.2% linked to US dollar trends, partly offset by the renminbi.

Cognac leads for Rémy

The Cognac division posted organic growth of 7.7% in the quarter, with performance varying sharply by region. In the Americas, sales saw a limited decline, which the group attributed to continued destocking in Canada and a high comparison base in Latin America, while the United States delivered solid performance.

The Asia-Pacific (APAC) was the standout region, with strong growth driven by solid momentum across the Rest of Asia. Sales in China were in "limited decline" which the group said was in line with expectations in a still-challenging market.

Liqueurs and spirits under pressure

The liqueurs and spirits division fell 6.6% organically. The Americas saw a slight decline, reflecting an unfavourable phasing effect following a strong rebound in shipments in the previous quarter. Performance across EMEA was mixed.

Overall, EMEA sales declined amid sustained competitive pressure and moderate consumer demand.

Breakdown of sales by division

In €m (April-June) Q1 2026-27 Q1 2025-26 Change as reported Organic change
Cognac 141.9 131.3 +8.1% +7.7%

Partner brands continued their steep decline, down 47.9% organically, though this represents a small share of overall group revenue and mainly reflected "the discontinuation of distribution of partner brands in the Benelux from April".

Rémy Cointreau said the results marked a start to the year in line with its expected full-year trajectory, and confirmed its objectives for 2026-27.
